title: The same stream
hookLine: the same stream of life that runs through my veins runs through the world (Gitanjali 69)
tomorrow: how long does a butterfly have, by Tagore's count?
last: SHE DANCED · STILL SUNG · SONG OFFERINGS.

cards: Most days a scrap of paper on the sidewalk is just litter. For Debendranath Tagore, the poet's father, one scrap was a turning point. He tells it in his autobiography.

As a young man, rich and restless, he saw a torn page of a Sanskrit book blow past him. He picked it up and couldn't make it all out, so he took it to a scholar. It was the opening of the Isha Upanishad.

teach.b: Its first line, in Sanskrit, is isha vasyam idam sarvam: all this, whatever moves in the world, is dwelt in by the Lord. Debendranath said those words changed his life, and he raised his son on the Upanishads.

Years later that son wrote Gitanjali's sixty-ninth song, which sounds like the same line, felt from the inside: "The same stream of life that runs through my veins night and day runs through the world and dances in rhythmic measures."

Then: "It is the same life that shoots in joy through the dust of the earth in numberless blades of grass and breaks into tumultuous waves of leaves and flowers." That's the teaching, from two voices.

teach.h: ALL THIS IS DWELT IN BY THE LORD.
teach.b: The Isha says the Lord dwells in all this. The song hears it from the inside, as one stream of life in everything, and in you.

teach.h: ONE STREAM IN VEINS AND GRASS.
teach.b: In the song, grass stays grass, and you stay you.
The stream makes them kin. Now look back at the week, and listen for the stream under it: Mira dancing where anyone could see. Songs passing from voice to voice.
A song offered like a flower. The vessel refilling, God standing in the field, a whole country waking without fear.
If the same stream runs through your pulse and the grass outside, then nothing ordinary is quite ordinary.

how: The Isha Upanishad is short enough to be memorized, and its opening verse is often recited; Gitanjali's songs are read aloud, and their Bengali originals sung as Rabindrasangeet.

s: the torn page Debendranath found was from the Isha Upanishad
its opening: all this, whatever moves in the world, is dwelt in by the Lord.
Gitanjali 69 says the stream of life runs only through people
the same life shoots through the dust in blades of grass, leaves and flowers.
Gitanjali 69 says grass and people stop being different things
the song hears one life in many forms: grass still shoots up as grass. kin, not erased.

games.q: your nephew asks why his grandma thanks the mango tree before picking its fruit. what could Gitanjali 69 give you to say at dinner?
o: the same life that runs in your veins runs in the tree, so she's greeting family.
trees can hear words, and good manners make their fruit grow sweeter.
it's an old habit with no meaning; she's just being polite.
games.why: Gitanjali 69: the same stream of life runs through the veins and the world. one life, many forms: kin.

practice: Put two fingers on the inside of your wrist until you find your pulse. Keep them there, and if there's a window or a breeze, notice the air moving too.
For two minutes, let the beat under your fingers and the moving air be one stream, as the song hears it.

wordCard.voice: The same stream: Gitanjali sixty-nine, the life in your veins running through the whole world, all of it dwelt in by one Lord.
